extracted.intended_audience: faculty and program designers who prepare middle school mathematics teachers; mathematics teacher educators and course authors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for designing, describing, and assessing pre-service and in-service programs and courses for middle school mathematics teachers, including required program/article elements, course outlines, learning goals, assessment practices, and sample grading rubrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Middle school teachers' mathematical content requirements (MET-derived)
rubrics_metrics.description: All middle school teachers need to know the mathematics content for elementary teachers. In addition: in the strand of number sense and operation, middle school teachers need to be fluent with the number line model for the real numbers, proportional reasoning, and elementary number theory; be able to distinguish among rational and irrational numbers and their representations. In the algebra strand, middle school teachers need to see algebra not simply as a generalization tool but also as a study of linear, polynomial, and exponential functions and as a body of techniques for equation solving. In the geometry strand, middle school teachers need to be proficient with transformational plane geometry, congruence and similarity, and connections of geometry to art and nature; they also need to be able to use a variety of strategies for developing and using formulas for areas of plane figures and volumes of polyhedra. In the strand of probability and statistics, middle school teachers need to experience the design and execution of a small statistics project, and get familiar with normal curves and sampling distributions, and the basis of inferential statistics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This description is presented as the core mathematical content teachers must master; course and program curricula should explicitly address these topics and representations. Use examples, projects (e.g., a small statistics project), and multiple representations to ensure conceptual understanding and connections to classroom practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical techniques recommended for middle school teacher preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some of the pedagogical techniques that facilitate the learning for middle school teachers are hands-on approaches, cooperative learning, effective classroom discourse, writing, and technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courses and programs should incorporate these instructional approaches frequently; course materials and sample activities should demonstrate how they are used to develop both content knowledge and pedagogical-content knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core Program Paper Outline (required components for program descriptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors were asked to incorporate as many components of the following outline into the description of their program as possible: I. Instructional Information (A. Size and location of school; B. Student participation in the program). II. Program History (A. Intended audience; B. Program beginning; C. Background and philosophy of the program). III. Degree Requirements (A. State requirements (in appendices); B. Learning goals and objectives (1. For the program; 2. For the courses); C. Certification tests; D. Courses requirements (1. Mathematics courses; 2. Mathematics education courses); E. Mathematics education courses (1. Instructor information; 2. Course list specifically for middle school mathematics teachers; 3. Enrollment for these courses; 4. Syllabi links; 5. Activities: a. Resources; b. Connection to classroom; c. Connection to program and course learning goals and objectives). IV. Assessment (A. Student reaction; B. Student employment perspective; C. Middle school administrators’ reactions; D. Student performance on required state examinations; E. Retention in education). V. References and links.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is effectively a rubric for what program-descriptive articles should include. Program authors should cover each listed area where applicable and include links or appendices for state requirements, syllabi, and assessment data to provide consistency across reported programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core Course Paper Outline (required components for course descriptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors were asked to incorporate as many components of the following outline into the descriptions of their courses as possible: I. Introduction and Background (A. Course history, development of course; B. Course structure; C. Prerequisite and enrollment information). II. Course materials and resources (A. Syllabi; B. Teaching Notes; C. Classroom materials). III. Course structure and format. IV. Course content. V. Essential course elements (possible) (A. Assignments; B. Student Experiences; C. Class Projects; D. Assessment). VI. References and links. VII. Appendices (possible) (A. Table of contents for author written materials; B. Assessment materials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Course articles should provide concrete artifacts when possible (syllabi, sample activities, assessments, instructor notes) and explicitly state learning objectives, core content, and course structure so others can adopt/adapt the course.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article submission/content expectation (common core information)
rubrics_metrics.description: While each article describes the unique program or course of its respective institution, each also includes a common core of information to provide some consistency to the volume. In particular, all articles describing middle school programs contain information about the host institution, a history of the program, degree and testing requirements for the program and for state licensure, learning goals and objectives for the program and courses, and any available assessment data. When applicable information is included about particular courses, for example, some articles provide sample activities or syllabi and some have a description of courses in the appendix. Most articles have links to websites containing further information about the program, courses, state requirements, or resources that can be downloaded and used directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program and course authors should aim for this common core to aid readers (faculty new to the area or seasoned teachers) in judging transferability and implementation feasibility at their home institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical knowledge goals (Math in the Middle / Adding It Up strands)
rubrics_metrics.description: A condensed Math in the Middle statement consistent with the five strands from the National Academy of Sciences report Adding It Up: 1. Conceptual Understanding; 2. Adaptive Reasoning; 3. Procedural Fluency; 4. Mathematical Problem Solving Competence; 5. Productive Disposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these five strands as strategic learning goals for courses: design activities, assessments, and reflections that cultivate conceptual understanding, reasoning, fluency, problem solving, and productive disposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course process objectives (Principles and Standards processes)
rubrics_metrics.description: From the view of the Principles and Standards for School Mathematics, the course’s strategic objectives focus on problem solving, reasoning, and proof and the associated processes: 1. Problem Solving; 2. Reasoning and Proof; 3. Communication; 4. Connections; 5. Representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Course content and assessments should emphasize these processes (e.g., write proofs, present solutions, make connections across topics, use multiple representations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Structured course activity sequence (session/sub-session pattern and tasks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pattern of activities in each sub-session: 1. Read the section of the textbook to prepare for reasoning, conjecturing, proving, and solving. 2. Complete the Pre-Test on the Web (five AMC problems; not for grading; diagnostic). 3. Complete the five assigned 'Solidifying Ideas' problems in the text and submit them for grading. 4. Complete the two 'New Ideas' problems in the text and submit solutions for grading. 5. Complete the assigned 'Habits of Mind' problem from the Further Challenges section and submit a solution. 6. A Post-Test (five AMC problems) drawn from same database as Pre-Test; can be retaken until mastery. Session Reflections: choose problems and write a one-page reflection about them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prescribes an evidence-based learning cycle: preview reading, low-stakes diagnostic, scaffolded practice of core problems, extension/challenge tasks, mastery checks, and reflective writing. Programs may adapt the exact numbers but should preserve the sequence and purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment components and grading breakdown (Math in the Middle example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Grading will be based on the work submitted for the Portfolio, the approximately weekly Solidifying Ideas, New Ideas, and Habits of Mind solutions, the Post-Tests, and the Essays on Proof. Each of the 10 or 11 sub-sessions has eight problems graded on a scale of '1' (good/satisfactory), '2' (better/noteworthy), and '3' (excellent/exemplary). Each sub-session worth up to 24 points; homework sub-sessions count for 50% of grade total. The seven Post-Tests count about 3.5% each (about 25% total). The Learning and Teaching Project and End-of-Course Problem set count about 10%; responses/critiques posted on Blackboard discussion lists count about 5%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide transparent point allocations, rubrics for homework quality, and allow mastery opportunities (Post-Test retakes). Include portfolio artifacts for summative assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Late work and redo policy (formative encouragement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Homework should be faxed to the Center Office on the due date. Any problem on which you receive a grade of '1' can be re-done, and resubmitted up to one week after the homework is returned for a re-grade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies should emphasize learning over punishment: allow re-dos within a limited window; provide feedback to guide improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectations for reading and writing in mathematics courses
rubrics_metrics.description: When you are asked to read or write something, the following is expected: Read so you can be an active participant in discussions of text. Write so you can respond to posed questions clearly and grammatically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructors should set explicit expectations for reading preparation and written communication quality; include feedback cycles to help teachers improve mathematical writing and discourse skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grading descriptors / achievement levels (course-level rubric language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expectations and typical characteristics of achievement at each grade level: AC — honorific and rare, evidence of exceptional command of mathematics, ability to transfer to classroom, far-reaching progress in educational inquiry. A — achievement beyond the level needed to earn BC; good command of mathematics, ability to transfer to classroom, progress in developing knowledge/skills/dispositions. BC — regular class attendance, active participation, assignments submitted on-time, supportive and helpful to peers, admirable effort and evidence of good progress. B — regular attendance, reasonable participation, most assignments on-time, cooperative, reasonable effort. Below B — indicates inadequate effort (attendance problems, uncooperative behavior, failure to submit assignments, late submissions, inadequate performance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide narrative descriptors for letter grades tied to observable behaviors (attendance, participation, timeliness) and to evidence of learning and classroom transfer. Use these descriptors to justify grades and give formative guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program/course assessment evidence types (what to report)
rubrics_metrics.description: When describing programs, include any available assessment data: student reaction, student employment perspective, middle school administrators’ reactions, student performance on required state examinations, retention in education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report both qualitative (student/administrator reactions, employment outcomes) and quantitative (exam scores, retention rates) measures; include assessment instruments or links in appendices where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course design pedagogy guidance (concrete practice and withholding outlines)
rubrics_metrics.description: For many topics, be concrete when explaining them. One technique: withhold the Course Outline initially so participants make conjectures and develop ideas before being given a formal list of theorems and properties. Distribute outline sections as they are completed. Use concrete analogies (e.g., the 'blue frog' counterexample) to make abstract concepts tangible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design courses to foster discovery and conjecture; control release of authoritative summaries to encourage student-led development; use concrete hooks and analogies to make abstract notions accessible to teacher-learners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor and assistant instructor roles and materials expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Assistant instructors duties include: lead class discussion of solutions from problem sessions; present specific algorithms or lessons (Euclidean algorithm, divisibility rules); lead small group problem sessions; grade daily homework and provide feedback; keep record of participant presentations; write theorems/definitions on poster paper; provide evening assistance. Provide assistant instructors with a copy of the course notebook and solutions prior to course start. Hard copies of solutions for instructors, but not participants, should be kept in instructor notebook.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify assistant instructor responsibilities and provide preparatory materials; delineate which materials are instructor-only to preserve discovery-based learning when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course artifacts and appendices to include
rubrics_metrics.description: When applicable, include sample activities, syllabi, teaching notes, class projects, assessment materials or course websites in appendices or via links. Authors often include sample syllabi and appendices (e.g., table of contents for course notes, assessment materials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide downloadable artifacts and concrete classroom-tested resources to facilitate adoption; appendices should contain reproducible materials (syllabi, problem sets, rubrics).
